rationale:
Every piece today is about GLP-1. We skipped anything we've covered in the last 30 days. That ruled out bootleg Reta, TRIUMPH-2, nails, muscle, the pilot trial on stopping, the pill vs shot, the surgery checklist, EloraTZP and HFpEF. We also skipped the schizophrenia story because we haven't found the underlying paper yet.

L1 is an evergreen deep-dive on the only randomized head-to-head trial so far, SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM 2025, peer-reviewed). It fits the format that works best for us: a named drug in a "X vs Y: which" title, with tirzepatide in it. The news hook is the current Wegovy HD indirect-comparison talk. Our 09-30 carousel covered that indirect comparison, so this is a different angle.

S1 is a spin-off of L1 with one number. S2 is a tirzepatide benefit-beyond-weight Short on diabetic eye disease. It's an early, low-competition story and it's observational, so we say "linked to". S3 busts the myth that there's an approved GLP-1 patch, the same format that worked for our online-retatrutide Short. C1 is a save-worthy checklist on pregnancy planning, built on the label and new evidence. It's a rising topic for the women 25–45 in our audience.

The mix is 1 evergreen-with-hook, 3 rising or emerging and 1 myth-bust. The pillars are results ×2, beyond-weight, myths and is-it-for-you. The topics cover weight results, eyes, how medicine is delivered and pregnancy, so no body system repeats.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide vs semaglutide in the only randomized head-to-head trial so far: SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM 2025), adults with obesity without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound) vs Semaglutide (Wegovy): Who Lost More in the Obesity Head-to-Head Trial?' (adults without diabetes are stated in the first spoken line). Hook: 'In Sept 2026 Lilly reported an indirect comparison against Wegovy HD. But one trial in adults with obesity and no diabetes actually randomized people to the two drugs.' Section 2 adds one line: 'An earlier trial, SURPASS-2, compared them in type 2 diabetes at lower semaglutide doses. That's a different population.' Everything else as planned. Every SURMOUNT-5 number carries the treatment-regimen estimand, 72 wk, arm (maximum tolerated dose) and comparator. Wegovy HD gets one line: 'FDA-approved Mar 19 2026, studied in STEP UP, a separate trial, not head-to-head.' Close with the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) vs Semaglutide (Wegovy): Which Lost More in the Head-to-Head Trial?
pieces.why: Fits our proven long-form format (named drugs, 'X vs Y: which', tirzepatide in the title) and rests on a peer-reviewed RCT that will pass the fact-check. Search demand for Zepbound vs Wegovy is rising. | fact-check: Verified: SURMOUNT-5 (Aronne et al., NEJM, May 11 2025). 751 randomized, open-label, Lilly-sponsored, maximum tolerated dose (tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg vs semaglutide 1.7 or 2.4 mg, weekly). LS-mean weight change at 72 wk was −20.2% vs −13.7% (about 22.8 kg vs 15.0 kg). Population: adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Wegovy HD (semaglutide 7.2 mg) was FDA-approved Mar 19 2026. Lilly's indirect comparison (SURMOUNT-1 vs STEP UP) was a press release on Sep 29 2026, presented at EASD 2026. MAJOR scope error: 'the only randomized head-to-head trial so far' is false. SURPASS-2 (NEJM 2021) randomized tirzepatide against semaglutide 1 mg in type 2 diabetes. It must read 'the only head-to-head trial in people with obesity WITHOUT diabetes' (or 'the obesity head-to-head'). Other fixes: (a) drop 'just released' from the hook. The press release is 2+ weeks old and news fades. Use 'In Sept 2026, Lilly reported an indirect comparison…', label it as a company press release, and give its estimand. (b) The doses in the trial arms are fine as arm labels. Never present 7.2 mg eligibility or step-up rules (the label's 'after tolerating 2.4 mg for 4 weeks') as instructions. (c) Copy waist change, ≥15%/≥25% shares, GI AEs and AE-related discontinuation per arm exactly from the NEJM paper, with the treatment-regimen estimand stated. (d) Keep 'Lilly-sponsored' in every caption. (e) The title must name the population. Include the 'not right for everyone' and 'don't stop or switch on your own' lines.

pieces.topic: SURMOUNT-5 in one number: tirzepatide vs semaglutide head to head
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide Head to Head: Who Lost More in 72 Weeks? #shorts' (no numbers in the title, answered by 10 s). Opening line: 'In the head-to-head trial in adults with obesity and no diabetes, people on tirzepatide lost about 20.2% of body weight on average at 72 weeks, vs 13.7% on semaglutide.' Pill: 'SURMOUNT-5 · NEJM 2025 · open-label · Lilly-sponsored · max tolerated doses · obesity, no diabetes'. Add one GI line with per-arm figures from the paper. Then 'Bigger average ≠ best for you. Tolerability and your health conditions matter. Don't switch or stop on your own.' End with the full-video pointer and the prescriber line. 170 words or fewer.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide Head to Head: 20.2% vs 13.7% #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 that drives traffic to the long video. Names both drugs in a comparison, and tirzepatide titles get a median of 90 views for us. | fact-check: Figures verified (NEJM 2025: −20.2% vs −13.7%, 72 wk, n=751, open-label, Lilly-sponsored, maximum tolerated dose). Problems: (1) 'the one head-to-head trial' is false without scope, because SURPASS-2 compared the two drugs in type 2 diabetes. (2) The title carries two numbers, against the at-most-one-number rule. It also omits the population and timeframe. (3) Name 'average' and the estimand ('treatment-regimen estimand' on the pill, or 'on average, everyone randomized'). (4) Copy GI AE rates and AE discontinuation for both arms from the paper. Don't just call them 'common'. Add the prescriber line plus 'don't switch or stop on your own'.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and diabetic eye disease: large cohort (n=173,846, Ophthalmology) linked tirzepatide to lower rates of diabetic retinopathy vs lifestyle intervention alone
pieces.angle: Title: 'Is Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Linked to Less Diabetic Eye Disease? #shorts'. Opening line by 10 s: 'A large health-records study linked tirzepatide to lower rates of diabetic eye disease over 12 months, vs lifestyle changes alone. Linked to, not proof.' On screen: 'adults with diabetes + overweight/obesity · 173,846 matched patients · 12 months · observational · Ophthalmology 2026'. Give absolute rates per arm from the paper. One line defining retinopathy. One calm line: 'Big, fast drops in blood sugar can briefly worsen retinopathy in some people, so if you already have it, tell your eye doctor and prescriber.' Action: keep regular diabetic eye exams. Brief GI side-effects line. Then 'Don't stop or change your current medicines on your own' and the prescriber line. No emoji.
pieces.working_title: Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Protect Your Eyes in Diabetes? #shorts
pieces.why: Fits our winning formula: a named drug, a 'what does it do to my body?' question and a practical action. Few creators cover it and it's framed as a benefit. Safety-scare framing underperforms for us, so we avoid it here. | fact-check: Verified: 'Tirzepatide and Reduced Risk of Diabetic Retinopathy and Related Complications: A Multicenter US Cohort Study', Ophthalmology 2026 (PubMed 41577258). Retrospective TriNetX cohort, propensity-matched, 173,846 patients (86,923 per arm). Adults with diabetes and overweight/obesity, vs lifestyle intervention alone with no exposure to weight-loss drugs. 12-month outcomes: incident or progressive DR and interventions (anti-VEGF, PRP). Issues: (1) the working title 'Protect Your Eyes' is causal and too reassuring for an observational study. Use 'linked to'. (2) State the 12-month window and that the comparator is a coded 'lifestyle intervention' group. Residual confounding is possible (people prescribed tirzepatide may differ in access and care). (3) Absolute risks per group must come from the paper's own table, not press coverage. If absolute rates aren't available, give no relative figure. (4) Be balanced. Fast drops in blood sugar have been linked to early worsening of retinopathy in some people, and a real-world cohort has examined early worsening on tirzepatide (PMC12361273). One calm line supports the eye-exam action, especially for people who already have retinopathy. That fits better than NAION. Leave NAION out. (5) Don't claim the drug works for eyes via weight or sugar unless the paper says so.

pieces.topic: Is there an approved GLP-1 patch? Real semaglutide and tirzepatide microneedle patches are still in development as of Oct 2026
pieces.angle: Title: 'Is There an Approved GLP-1 Patch Yet? (As of Oct 2026) #shorts'. Opening line by 10 s: 'Is there an approved GLP-1 patch? Not yet, as of Oct 2026.' Explain that semaglutide is a big peptide that the skin barrier mostly keeps out, so researchers are testing microneedle patches. Example: Daewoong's semaglutide patch is in early (phase 1) testing in Korea, and the company is aiming for manufacturing-site (GMP) approval in H1 2027, which is not drug approval. Patches sold online as 'GLP-1 patches' aren't the approved medicines. FDA warns about unapproved GLP-1 products. Better route: ask your prescriber about approved pill or injection options. No tirzepatide patch claim, no seller, no product shots. Close with the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Is There a GLP-1 Patch Yet? What's Real in 2026 #shorts
pieces.why: Myth-busts about unapproved online products work for us (online-retatrutide Short 56, 'cures online' Short 82). Competition is low and search pages are just appearing. | fact-check: Verified: Daewoong is targeting H1 2027 GMP approval of a microneedle facility (Hwaseong) to make DWRX5003, a once-weekly semaglutide patch (Korea Biomedical Review idxno=33474; Korea Herald). Korea's MFDS cleared a phase 1 trial in Oct 2025. The GMP target is for manufacturing clinical-trial supply and, later, commercial supply. It is NOT a product approval, so say so. The company-reported '>80% bioavailability vs injection' is a company claim. Use it only if credited and labelled early-stage, or leave it out. A separate semaglutide microarray patch study (VX-201 vs subcutaneous injection, NCT07673900) is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov. I could not verify any tirzepatide patch developer. Search results were dominated by gray-market seller pages, so drop the tirzepatide developer line entirely. Myth-bust format fits the playbook (online 'retatrutide' 56). Never show, name or describe sellers, and don't show realistic product imagery. Cite FDA's 'FDA's concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs used for weight loss' page directly (verify the canonical URL at script stage).

pieces.topic: Planning a pregnancy on semaglutide or tirzepatide: what the labels, the new international consensus and a Sept 2026 meta-analysis say
pieces.angle: 'Planning a Pregnancy on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? Questions to Bring to Your Prescriber'. Slide 2: 'Weight loss may affect fertility, and some early studies in PCOS suggest changes in ovulation. Early evidence, not a fertility treatment.' Use a confirmed source or drop the claim. Slide 3: '10 observational studies: no clearly detectable increase in [outcomes listed], but authors say this does not establish safety or support use in pregnancy.' Slide 4: verbatim label line plus revision date, framed as 'label guidance to review with your prescriber'. Slide 5: verbatim tirzepatide contraception line plus revision date, plus 'ask your prescriber which method fits you'. Slide 6: the Lancet OGWH consensus, labelled 'in women with type 1, type 2 or gestational diabetes'. Slide 7: prescriber/OB-GYN questions, including 'If I become pregnant unexpectedly, who do I call first?' and 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own; call your prescriber.' Slide 8: the prescriber line. No 'Ozempic babies', no emoji hook.
pieces.working_title: Planning a Pregnancy on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? What Labels and New Evidence Say
pieces.why: Rising topic with fresh primary sources (meta-analysis, consensus, JCEM) that matters to the women 25–45 in our audience. A checklist people will want to save, and the topic hasn't been covered in 30 days. | fact-check: Topic is allowed and useful, but sensitive. Verified: the 'no clearly detectable increase' meta-analysis is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 observational studies in 2,118,215 women (8,325 exposed within 6 months before a positive pregnancy test). The authors explicitly say the findings 'do not establish safety or support continued use during pregnancy' and 'may offer limited reassurance'. That limit must appear on the same slide. Note the EMJ write-up lists the journal as 'Medicine'. Confirm journal, date (Sept 2026?) and DOI from the paper itself, and cite the paper, not EMJ. International consensus verified: Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health 2026, 'Preconception, pregnancy, and postnatal use of GLP-1 receptor agonist-based therapies in women with type 1, type 2, or gestational diabetes…'. Its population is women WITH DIABETES. It must not be presented as guidance for people using GLP-1s for weight without diabetes. NOT verified: a 'JCEM 2026' PCOS fertility paper. The only 2026 item I found was a JBRA Assisted Reproduction narrative review. The writer must locate and confirm the JCEM paper or drop slide 2's citation. Labels: quote the current Wegovy/Ozempic PI wording ('discontinue … at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy') with the revision date, credited as label text. Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) oral-contraceptive note: quote the label verbatim with the revision date. Don't paraphrase it into dose-escalation instructions. Packaging: avoid 'fertility boost' framing and anything that implies GLP-1s as a fertility treatment (off-label). Analytics note for the owner: carousels reach 0–3 accounts. Consider rebuilding as a Short later, but that isn't a safety issue.
